ai-158994b8ae.headline: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
ai-158994b8ae.fulltext:
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

world-c7f2c0279d.headline: Bahrain says Iranian attack hits industrial facility as air defences intercept attacks
world-c7f2c0279d.fulltext:
[Text below is Al Jazeera's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Bahrain says Iranian attack causes fire at industrial facility
Bahrain reports no injuries, as Iran’s IRGC says it targeted US military positions at two bases in al-Riffa and Awali.
Bahrain says an Iranian attack has struck a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire, in the latest escalation of the war in the Middle East.
Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defences intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks late on Saturday.
In a post on X, Bahrain’s Ministry of Interior said the attack was part of “Iranian aggression”.
It said preliminary reports pointed to material damage but no injuries, and that civil defence teams were working to bring the fire under control.
The Interior Ministry did not name the facility or say where it was. Earlier, air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain, and the ministry urged residents to move to the nearest safe place without saying what the threat was.
In a statement after the attack, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting United States military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain.
The IRGC claimed it destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
The attack was “in response to continued aggression and violations of the airspace of the Islamic Republic of Iran”, the statement said.
“After two US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones violated Iranian airspace, US military positions at the aforementioned bases were targeted in an operation by the IRGC Aerospace Force,” it added.
Earlier, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported that the IRGC had attacked two military bases used by US forces at Sheikh Isa and Juffair.
The IRGC said that operation, as well as being in response to continued violations of Iranian airspace, came following a US attack on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island.
Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain had also crashed on Sitra Island and started a large fire. It cited an outlet called Bahrain News, which blamed a recurring malfunction in the Patriot air defence system.
Bahrain hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. It has been attacked repeatedly since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February, including three drone attacks in recent days after a lull of several weeks.
Other Gulf states have also come under repeated fire from Tehran since the US-Israel war began.
Reactions to latest Iranian strikes
In a statement on X, Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry called on the United Nations Security Council to take “firm measures to compel Iran” to implement Resolution 2817.
The resolution, adopted on March 11, condemns Iranian attacks against Gulf states and Jordan, and demands an immediate halt to hostilities and maritime interference.
The head of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) expressed his “full solidarity” with Bahrain following Iran’s attack on the industrial facility.
Jassim Mohamed AlBudaiwi, GCC secretary-general, said Bahrain’s security, territorial integrity, facilities, citizens and residents are an integral part of the security of the GCC states, and that the council stands united in confronting threats to their security and stability.
The GCC backs “all measures” Bahrain takes to deal with the attack, he added.

world-86c4e81769.headline: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
world-86c4e81769.fulltext:
Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
- Published
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

world-286cc01f5f.headline: Deadly attack in Kyiv as Russia launches barrage against Ukraine
world-286cc01f5f.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
world-286cc01f5f.fulltext:
[Text below is Time Magazine's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Russia launched a barrage of drones and missiles at Kyiv in what Ukrainian officials described as a “night of horror” for the capital.
At least 25 people have been killed, according to the State Emergency Service of Ukraine, and more than 80 injured. Search and rescue efforts are still underway.
“Russia launched more than 70 missiles of various types against Ukraine overnight, nearly half of them ballistic missiles, along with almost 500 attack drones, including jet-powered shaheds,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday.
Strikes were reported at more than 30 locations across every district of Kyiv, including residential neighborhoods, driving citizens into bomb shelters and underground metro stations.
Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko has declared a day of mourning, with flags on municipal buildings set to be flown at half-mast.
The Sumy, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Cherkasy, and Kharkiv areas were also impacted.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the assault as a "night of horror" and referred to Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “war criminal.”
“Putin can only wage a vile and terroristic war against civilians, women, and children. Because in his war against Ukraine’s Defense Forces he cannot achieve a single result,” he argued.
The Russian Defense Ministry declared the “massive attack” was carried out in response to Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russia.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the assault had been aimed at "military or military-related facilities" and vowed Russia will "continue increasing pressure" on Ukraine in order to achieve its goals.
Ukraine has stepped up its drone attacks on oil refineries, with reports indicating Russia is now entering a summer fuel crisis.
Last week, Zelensky “approved a 40-day influence operation” for the Security Service of Ukraine “against the aggressor state, aimed at compelling it to end the war.”
The Ukrainian leader was in Dublin, Ireland, on Monday, discussing Ukraine’s envisioned future in the E.U. as Ireland assumed the presidency of the European Council on Wednesday, but he cut short his visit and returned home, relaying he had received intel about “another massive Russian strike.”
Following the assault, European leaders have repledged their support to Ukraine and its people.
“Russia has again chosen escalation over peace with this deplorable onslaught on Kyiv, including dozens of missiles and hundreds of drones killing and injuring civilians, including children,” said U.K. Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper. “We will keep increasing the international pressure on Russia, strengthen Ukraine’s air defences—solidarity with Ukraine.”
Irish Minister of State Thomas Byrne described the overnight attacks as showing Russia’s “utter brutality and inhumanity” and said Ireland will stand with Ukraine “for however long it takes.”
Kaja Kallas, the E.U.'s chief diplomat, said “words of condemnation alone will not stop attacks on Kyiv. Only sustained military support for Ukraine and increased pressure on Moscow can do that.”
“Today, I will propose to sanction more entities supporting Russia’s military-industrial complex in response to the strikes. The more Moscow attacks civilians, the more sanctions must be imposed,” she vowed.
On Tuesday, the E.U. disbursed the first installment of its €6 billion defense package to support drone procurement as part of the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan.
Zelensky thanked European partners for their ongoing support when he visited an area of Kyiv struck in the overnight attack, but raised concerns about the speed of U.S. aid.
When asked about the U.S. providing more ballistic defenses, Zelensky told reporters: "We are thankful to the American team for the transfer of these missiles. But for for today, it's too slow."
He added: "We are asking President [Donald] Trump, his team... rush."
Meanwhile, Marta Kos, the European commissioner for enlargement, has said the assault highlights why “Ukraine needs the means to defend itself and a credible path to E.U. membership.”
Is Ukraine joining the European Union?
Ukraine is a step closer to joining the European Union, after officials opened the first negotiating cluster last month—initiating a crucial phase of the membership negotiation process.
Zelensky has long framed Ukraine’s bid to join the E.U. as a way to bolster its security guarantees amid attacks from Russia.
Despite strong political support from some European leaders, Ukraine faces a long, complex path before membership of the bloc becomes a reality. Zelensky's eagerness to have the decision on accession fast-tracked by 2027 has been met with skepticism.
Since formally applying for membership in 2022, shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has made significant progress toward meeting E.U. member state requirements and has continued aligning its laws and regulations with E.U. standards through the Association Agreement framework.
While last month's opening negotiations mark a significant milestone for Ukraine, many hurdles remain.
Accession negotiations are divided into six clusters, with the first cluster considered the most important. Known as the “fundamentals” cluster, it focuses on democracy, rule of law, governance, and judicial reform.
Overall, the decision of E.U. enlargement ultimately stands with the member states. Throughout the accession process, every cluster must be opened and closed unanimously.
Attitudes toward Ukraine’s membership varies across Europe.
Countries such as Germany and France both reportedly support a faster “symbolic” membership for Ukraine and have generally been more supportive of Ukraine’s aspirations.
Others remain more cautious. Even under its new leadership, Hungary has signaled opposition to any effort to fast-track Ukraine into the bloc.

India's Solar Cell Capacity May Double Expected Demand by FY27, Putting Pressure on Manufacturers' Margins: YES Securities
Updated: Nov 21, 2026 01:12:57pm
India's Solar Cell Capacity May Double Expected Demand by FY27, Putting Pressure on Manufacturers' Margins: YES Securities
New Delhi, Nov 21 (KNN) India's solar manufacturing sector is approaching a major shift as new domestic cell capacity is expected to ease supply shortages and reduce the price premium for locally produced cells, putting pressure on manufacturers' profitability, according to a YES Securities report.
The report said the industry was moving from module-led expansion towards a phase where ownership of cell manufacturing capacity would increasingly determine profitability, reported by ANI.
A major increase in cell supply is expected from the second half of FY27, while forward prices for domestic content requirement (DCR) modules have already started declining. "With a large cell supply wave due from H2FY27 and forward DCR prices already moving lower, we believe the sector is entering a phase where execution, integration and balance-sheet strength will separate the winners," the report said.
Cell Supply Expected to Exceed Demand
YES Securities estimates that India's cell manufacturing capacity could reach around 124 GW by FY27, against expected demand of nearly 60 GW. FY28 DCR module prices for independent power producers are estimated at around Rs 20 per watt peak (Wp), reflecting the expected price correction.
Profitability already varies significantly across manufacturers. Cell-integrated companies reported an aggregate EBITDA margin of around 31 percent in Q2 FY27, compared with 17.6 percent for partly integrated players and 7.7 percent for module-only manufacturers.
As of September 2026, India's module manufacturing capacity stood at around 204.9 GW, while cell capacity was 57.1 GW. Cell production lines operated at 81-99 percent utilisation in Q2, compared with 44-68 percent for module lines.
Weak Project Awards Pose Demand Risks
The report also flagged challenges on the demand side. New renewable energy awards fell to 14.7 GW in FY26 from 40.6 GW in FY25, while 40-45 GW of awarded capacity was yet to secure power purchase agreements. Solar power curtailment reached 8,133 GWh during April-June 2026.
Although a construction pipeline of over 150 GW could support demand through FY28, weaker project awards may affect volumes in FY29 and FY30.
US Duties Weigh on Export Opportunities
The report said US trade duties had made exports from India uneconomical, increasing the importance of domestic demand and manufacturing facilities located in the US.
"Exports from India to the US have become uneconomic following AD/CVD duties of 249 percent," it said.
The report added that timely commissioning of new cell facilities, capacity utilisation and cost management would determine which manufacturers could sustain margins as domestic supply increases.
(KNN Bureau)

science-mind-efaa63624f.headline: BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey
science-mind-efaa63624f.fulltext:
After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury. It is only the second mission — after NASA’s MESSENGER in 2011–2015 — to enter orbit around the innermost planet of the Solar System.
On 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres. In the coming weeks, its two scientific probes — one built by ESA and the other by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will separate, allowing each to follow its own orbit at a different altitude.
En route to Mercury the craft was able to test some of its onboard instruments. Mission scientists pointed the onboard X-ray camera, the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), at the Crab Nebula, the remnants of a supernova witnessed on Earth in 1054. MIXS is the first X-ray imaging device to be sent on an interplanetary mission, says Emma Bunce, a plasma physicist at the University of Leicester, UK, who is one of BepiColombo’s leading mission scientists.
One mission, two orbiters
For the time being, the two probes will remain conjoined, until they reach the prescribed orbit for the JAXA probe, called MIO, on 9 December. It will trace ellipses at altitudes between 500 km and 11,000 km, sampling the planet’s magnetic field and how it interacts with solar wind. The ESA-built probe, which is called Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and carries MIXS, among other instruments, will then gradually descend until March 2027, when it will reach its orbit at between 400–1,500 km. From there, its instruments will continuously study the planet’s surface.
Travelling to the Solar System’s innermost regions is a “prolonged affair”, Bunce says. “Energetically, it takes more energy to go to Mercury than to go to the outer Solar System,” says Bunce. BepiColombo launched in October 2018, and needed to gradually lower itself closer to the Sun without gaining speed and overshooting Mercury.

ai-9c9ec1c5f1.headline: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
ai-9c9ec1c5f1.fulltext:
Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
Key Points
- Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and the AI model Claude presented a proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, publishing it in the Lean programming language for computer verification.
- Just hours later, Stanford University researchers published an independent, entirely human approach to the same problem by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.
- Open since 1859, the hypothesis is central to understanding prime numbers, and confirming it would validate hundreds of dependent mathematical theories while underscoring AI's role in research.
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.
Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," he wrote in his announcement.
According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well.
Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line.
To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line.
Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says.
Stanford mathematicians rush out an all-human competing proof
Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement" on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.
"It is all human, with no AI," Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said.
Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away.
About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)," Vakil wrote.
Why both proofs could hold up and what happens next
Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them. Masullo's traditional proof comes with months of vetting by Brian Conrad, while Alpöge backs his AI proof with full computer verification.
Printed out, Claude's argument would run over 250,000 pages, Alpöge says, because the AI spells out even basic rules, such as a number other than one-half being either larger or smaller than one-half. To spare mathematicians that wall of text, Alpöge released the proof only in the Lean programming language, split into 14 data packages.
Lean acts like a digital referee, checking step by step whether every logical deduction follows from math's basic rules without errors or unproven assumptions. Human error is still possible if the original question was translated into code incorrectly at the start, though checking whether Alpöge coded the starting problem correctly should not take experts long, according to Scientific American. Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps.
Alpöge admits Claude was so far ahead of him in some complex subfields that he is presenting a result whose surrounding math he has not fully mastered yet. He expects the massive AI proof can be shortened quickly and plans to write a human-readable version over the coming months.
Anthropic's announcement also lands in a high-stakes business week, just a day after the company's major IPO on Thursday. Alpöge says he made the breakthrough late Sunday night and then contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for clearance. He calls the timing right after the public debut extremely unfortunate, but rejects any suggestion of a PR stunt, saying waiting any longer to publish simply was not an option.
This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which Claude has already solved several open math problems. In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a major release of results. Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof.
Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers
Journalist Joseph Howlett traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems."
At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics.
Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate.
Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime. His tool is the Riemann zeta function, which works like a calculating machine over a two-dimensional map with horizontal and vertical axes. Feed the machine a point's coordinates, and it outputs a new value. At certain points the result is exactly zero. Mathematicians call these points zeros.
Riemann saw that these zeros explain the apparent chaos of primes. Much like breaking a musical note into individual sound waves or overtones, the zeros correct Gauss's estimation error. Each zero acts like an instrument in an orchestra, with its vertical position setting the pitch and its horizontal position setting the volume.
Because calculating infinitely many points one by one was impossible, Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all the key zeros, known as non-trivial zeros, lie on a single vertical line at the horizontal value of one-half. "The Riemann hypothesis says all these different instruments in the orchestra of the primes play at exactly the same volume," Rutgers University's Alex Kontorovich explains. Apparent randomness turns into strict harmony.
A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role
If at least one of the two proofs holds up, number theorists would gain perfect control over how primes are distributed across the entire number line. Because a proof seemed unreachable for so long, mathematicians worked ahead for decades. Hundreds of papers assume the Riemann hypothesis is true, according to Kontorovich, and all of those theories would become established theorems overnight. Since both Alpöge's AI method and Masullo's work cover the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the breakthrough would also extend to fields ranging from simple equations to high-dimensional geometry.
The links also reach into computer science and physics. Prime numbers form the foundation of modern digital encryption. In 1972, physicist Freeman Dyson accidentally discovered over tea with a mathematician that the spacing of Riemann's zeros matches the energy levels inside atomic nuclei. That same formula keeps showing up in random particle motion, chaos theory, and black hole calculations.
Before this sudden double breakthrough, the field had hit a wall. Aside from quiet efforts like Masullo and Conrad's, almost no top mathematicians worked directly on the problem because they lacked a starting point. Two years ago, Oxford's James Maynard and MIT's Larry Guth showed that not too many points can stray far from Riemann's line. Though the biggest advance in decades, it struck Maynard himself and colleagues like Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal as only a minor improvement and stopgap.
That made the prospect of an AI cracking the puzzle all the more daunting. At a Harvard University workshop in October 2024, MIT number theorist Andrew Sutherland summed up the stakes. "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."
Even if Masullo's work saves human pride in this head-to-head race, models like Claude have changed fast. In just a year, they have gone from unreliable tools to systems that break through deep roadblocks and push the math community into an identity crisis. Alpöge still feels a mix of sadness at losing a 150-year-old guiding star and optimism about what comes next. "But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

deep-tech-e24a2ccff4.fulltext:
KOSPI Breaks Below 4,870 as Semiconductor Fears Prompt Brokerages to Leave 4,300 Level Open
Investor anxiety is mounting over the weekend after South Korea's stock market suffered a "Black Friday" and New York markets collapsed in a massive selloff. With the KOSPI pushed below the 4,900 level, brokerages are citing the 4,300 level as the lower bound of their additional-decline scenarios.
According to the Korea Exchange on the 22nd, the KOSPI closed at 4,869.96 on the 20th, down 5.21% from the previous trading day. The Kosdaq also fell 5.71% to close at 645.68. Sell-side sidecars were triggered on both markets, and foreign investors and institutions net-sold 1.132 trillion won (approximately $840.9 million) and 951.3 billion won (approximately $706.7 million) worth of KOSPI shares, respectively. Individuals, meanwhile, absorbed the volume with net purchases in the 2 trillion won (approximately $1.5 billion) range.
The decline was concentrated in large-cap semiconductor stocks. Samsung Electronics fell in the 7% range, SK Hynix around 6%, and Samsung Electro-Mechanics dropped more than 12%. Other top market-cap stocks such as SK Square and Samsung Life Insurance also weakened across the board, while LG Energy Solution and KB Financial Group saw relatively limited declines.
The bigger problem was the U.S. market, which opened after the South Korean market closed. On the 20th (local time), the Nasdaq plunged 5.28%, erasing all of this year's gains, while the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 3.70% and 1.93%, respectively. The S&P 500 declined for seven consecutive trading sessions. The VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, spiked to 35.89, its highest level since April of last year.
Semiconductor stocks were hit especially hard. Nvidia plunged 14.01%, while major names such as Micron (-13.89%), AMD (-13.25%), and Broadcom (-12.19%) all posted double-digit declines. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index also fell 10.73%. That is why observers expect selling pressure to be applied again to South Korean semiconductor stocks on Monday.
What makes this decline unusual is that stocks are failing to rebound even on positive news. Despite Nvidia's strong earnings and the successful IPO of Anthropic, AI investment sentiment has not recovered. Doubts remain over the massive funding and profitability needed for data center investment, and news that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices added to the concerns. Anthropic, which rose more than 17% on its first trading day, closed down 8.50% the following day.
Note: Based on U.S. market closing prices on the 20th (local time)
Brokerages' views are mixed. BNK Investment & Securities presented the KOSPI's 4,500 level as its worst-case scenario, while Hana Securities left the 4,300 level open. The calculation assumes that the price-to-book ratio (PBR) based on the past 12 months' earnings falls from the current 1.07 times to 0.94 times, the level of August last year before semiconductor stocks came into focus, implying a further decline of about 11.7% from the 20th's closing price.
What ultimately determines the index's direction is semiconductors. Of the amount by which the KOSPI's market capitalization has shrunk from its peak this year, about 68% came from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The two stocks' share of total market capitalization has fallen from 59% at the peak to 49%, but it still stands at nearly half. That means that unless large-cap semiconductor stocks find stability, volatility across the entire index will be hard to calm.
The scale of the correction itself, however, is already historic. The KOSPI has fallen about 47% from this year's peak. That exceeds the 44% maximum decline during the COVID-19 pandemic and approaches the 55% seen during the global financial crisis. Among KOSPI 200 constituents, 81% have fallen more than 40% from their peaks. Foreign investors net-sold 168 trillion won (approximately $124.8 billion) from May through November of this year, with the scale of selling relative to market capitalization approaching global financial crisis levels.
Interest rates are drawing attention as a clue to a rebound. The analysis suggests that if funds move into bonds amid the stock market plunge, government bond yields could fall, and a decline in rates at a time when corporate earnings forecasts have not been significantly damaged could serve as a trigger for a stock market rebound. Indeed, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield on the 20th briefly fell below 5% during intraday trading as demand for safe-haven assets strengthened.
Next week is packed with events that will gauge the sustainability of AI investment and the direction of interest rates. AI server demand and investment profitability can be confirmed in earnings reports from Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) on the 23rd and Dell on the 24th. The U.S. October Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, to be released on the 25th, is cited as a variable that will determine concerns over further tightening by the Federal Reserve. On the 26th, the Bank of Korea Monetary Policy Board meets.
Seo Sang-young, an executive director at Mirae Asset Securities, said, "Given that the U.S. stock market plunged, market anxiety remains high, so foreign investor flows will be important," adding, "Since the recent decline was heavily influenced by AI credit risk and supply-demand burdens, if related concerns ease, bargain-hunting led by semiconductors could flow in."
Han Ji-young, a researcher at Kiwoom Securities, noted that buying sentiment has weakened as stocks keep sliding even on positive catalysts such as Nvidia's strong earnings or Anthropic's listing. Cho A-in, a researcher at Samsung Securities, said mid- to long-term investment appeal remains valid but volatility may continue for the time being, proposing a staggered buying approach focused on quality stocks that have fallen excessively relative to earnings. Lim Jung-eun and Tae Yoon-sun, researchers at KB Securities, suggested that pessimism toward Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix may be nearing its peak, while emphasizing that caution is warranted over widening volatility ahead of key indicators and policy events.

india-8a6c9eb745.fulltext:
The emergence of Nagaur MP Hanuman Beniwal’s Rashtriya Loktantrik Party (RLP) as a strong third force in Panchayati Raj elections in Rajasthan has added a new dimension to the political contest ahead of the 2028 State Assembly election. The regional party has made a mark by surpassing 6% vote share in the polls.
Also read | Split INDIA bloc and ruling BJP face bypoll challenge in Rajasthan
With the victory at 497 panchayat samiti seats and 51 zila parishad seats, the RLP has demonstrated a significant rural presence. The party has showcased its strength by securing triumph not only in its stronghold of Nagaur, but also in Bikaner, Jodhpur, Churu, Didwana-Kuchaman, Barmer and even Sanganer in the State Capital, Jaipur.
Significantly, Sanganer is the Assembly constituency represented by Chief Minister Bhajan Lal Sharma. Across the State, the eight-year-old RLP secured 6.78% of the total votes polled for panchayat samiti seats and 6.64% of the votes cast for zila parishad members in the results announced on Friday.
The performance marks a significant expansion from the 2020 rural elections, when the RLP, then allied with Bharatiya Janata Party, won 60 panchayat samiti seats and 10 zila parishad seats in the main round. This time, the party has received more votes than the BJP in Nagaur and is poised to secure the Zila Pramukh post.
The party was reduced to a single seat in the 2023 Assembly election, when Mr. Beniwal won in Nagaur district’s Khinvsar. Subsequently, his wife and party candidate Kanika Beniwal lost to BJP in the bypoll held after his resignation on his election to Lok Sabha in 2024. The RLP has at present no member in the State Assembly.
A former BJP MLA and a vocal critic of former CM Vasundhara Raje, Mr. Beniwal, 54, had formed the RLP in 2018 with the support of Jats, who constitute a politically powerful community in more than a dozen Lok Sabha constituencies in Rajasthan. The BJP entered into an alliance with the RLP in the 2019 Lok Sabha election, when Mr. Beniwal was fielded and won from the Nagaur seat.
The RLP quit the NDA and withdrew its support to the BJP-led government at the Centre in December 2020 after the passage of the controversial agriculture sector Bills in the Parliament. Earlier, the party had contested at 57 seats in the 2018 Assembly election and won in three constituencies.
In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, Mr. Beniwal defeated BJP candidate Jyoti Mirdha, who is also a prominent Jat leader and the former Nagaur MP during 2009-2014. Ms. Mirdha, the grand-daughter of veteran Congress leader and former Union Minister, the late Nathuram Mirdha, had joined the BJP in September 2023 ahead of the Assembly election.
According to the political observers, Mr. Beniwal has recalibrated his strategy following the RLP’s dismal performance in the 2023 Assembly polls by attempting to expand the party through leveraging of mass movements and gaining popularity among the youth and farming communities.
In Jaipur, Mr. Beniwal organised a ‘Yuva Aakrosh Maharally’ and a sit-in protest demanding the cancellation of the 2021 sub-inspector recruitment exam and restructuring of the Rajasthan Public Service Commission. He spearheaded a ‘Yuva Hunkar Maharally’ in Jodhpur to protest against the Agnipath scheme and demand restoration of regular recruitment in the Armed Forces.
In his stronghold of Nagaur, Mr. Beniwal challenged the administration over issues such as compensation for farmers, crop insurance, agricultural power connections and illegal sand mining. He also extended support to ‘Save Bhairana Dham’ movement in Jaipur district’s Bichoon, protesting against a proposal to establish an industrial zone in the area.
At the national level, the RLP has sought to be in the limelight by maintaining political momentum and supporting various outfits. In New Delhi, Mr. Beniwal supported Arvind Kejriwal’s demand to include Jats across the country in the Central list of OBCs and joined the Cockroach Janta Party’s protest at Jantar Mantar in July this year.
In a statement issued here on Saturday, Mr. Beniwal hailed the panchayat election results as a proof of the RLP’s growing grassroots strength and a crucial step towards the 2028 Assembly election. “I trust that you will work for development of rural areas, help resolve common people’s issues and raise the voices of marginalised sections of society,” he told the elected representatives. India and Canada have wrapped up the sixth round of negotiations for their proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), with both sides pushing for an ambitious and balanced trade pact to expand market access, boost investments and strengthen economic ties. The talks, held in New Delhi from November 11 to 20, concluded on Friday, with progress reported across key areas of trade and investment.

The proposed pact is expected to open up additional opportunities for trade and investment. 
It also aims to strengthen resilient and diversified supply chains between the two countries.
The sixth round began with a meeting between Union commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal and Canada's minister of international trade Maninder Sidhu in New Delhi on November 11.
Both ministers emphasised the need for a balanced and mutually beneficial agreement. They said it should provide meaningful market access, build on the complementary strengths of the two economies and create fresh opportunities for trade and investment.
The ministers also reviewed the progress of negotiations and guided their respective teams to advance discussions constructively, the ministry said.
The Indian negotiating team was led by chief negotiator Brij Mohan Mishra, while the Canadian side was headed by chief negotiator Mary-Catherine Speirs.
The ministry said substantive discussions took place across various negotiating tracks during the latest round, with both sides making progress towards advancing the proposed agreement.
The negotiations are guided by the shared objective of concluding the pact within the ambitious timelines envisaged by the leaders of both countries, the release added.

IISER Pune Startup Develops Atomic Clock for Navigation
As of 21 November 2026, QuPrayog, a deep-tech startup incubated at the I-HUB Quantum Technology Foundation at IISER Pune, has developed a laboratory-scale atomic clock prototype using rubidium-87 atoms. The prototype was completed in seven months.
Prototype performance
Laboratory tests recorded frequency stability of about 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ over one second, improving to around 2 × 10⁻¹¹ over 100 to 1,000 seconds. Over 1,000 seconds, the prototype improved the stability of an ordinary crystal oscillator by about 50 times.
Development plans and support
Founded in 2024 by Dr Jay Mangaonkar and Dr Rahul Sawant, QuPrayog is also incubated at the IIT Madras Incubation Cell. It aims to launch a miniature version by August 2027 and plans compact, rugged clocks for satellite navigation, telecommunications and scientific instruments, while exploring optical atomic clock technology. Its technology development is supported by India’s deep-tech ecosystem, including the National Quantum Mission, approved in 2023 with an allocation of ₹6,003.65 crore over eight years for indigenous quantum technologies, including quantum sensing and precision measurement.
Important Facts for Exams
- Atomic resonance: Atomic clocks measure time by monitoring resonant frequencies associated with transitions between atoms’ quantised energy levels.
- SI time standard: The SI second is defined through the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of caesium-133, fixed at 9,192,631,770 hertz.
- Clock stability: Clock stability describes performance averaged over time to reduce the effects of noise and short-term fluctuations.
- Isotope decay: Rubidium-87 is radioactive, with a half-life of about 49.7 billion years, and beta-decays into stable strontium-87.

FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
- Published
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.
"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," Trump added.
This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyber-attacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with Trump saying he was not good enough.
Dan Lorhmann, a former analyst for the National Security Agency (NSA), told the BBC News Channel that the NCIC's data included "critical information relating to nationwide criminal activity" and needed to be protected.
He added that while US security agencies including the FBI have "an amazing ability" to keep such information safe" and are "globally respected", the level of cyber-attacks is rising globally.
"There's a lot of different reasons why that's happening but I do have faith in our experts in government," Lorhmann said.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

world-398adce4c4.headline: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
world-398adce4c4.fulltext:
China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.
At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.
But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.
In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”
Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.
While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.
But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.
Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.
Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.
China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.
One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.
Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”
China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.
Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.
Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”
Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”
Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

science-mind-9a7d621603.headline: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
science-mind-9a7d621603.fulltext:
AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
- Date:
- November 21, 2026
- Source:
- York University
- Summary:
- AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.
For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI
The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.
If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.
"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.
Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.
AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.
This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.
"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.
The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.
That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.
"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.
Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior
The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.
If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.
"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.
Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.
The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.
Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain
Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.
By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.
"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."
A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.
To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.
Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.
The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

science-mind-88875db0d1.headline: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
science-mind-88875db0d1.fulltext:
A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
- Date:
- November 21, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.
- Share:
Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a new lease on life.
Researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.
Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.
"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing."
How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion
For thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.
Once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.
The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.
"We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!"
Scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.
"When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space."
A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome
This kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.
As the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.
For Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.
But such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.
These surviving systems are important because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.
Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.
Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb
To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.
The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.
The simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.
Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Big Bao."
"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.
The researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.
At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.
Further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.
Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De said.
The merger has left astronomers with another important question: What is Bao like now?
The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.
Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs
One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.
Although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.
The researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.)
The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.
Earlier records showed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.
By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) showed further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.
Another important development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.
The telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.
Then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.
Scientists quickly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable new measurements.
Webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.
A New Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars
The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an important advance in the study of stellar mergers.
Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.
That timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.
The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.
NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.
One of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.
With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.
"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar said.
The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.
The James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.
Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).
