climate-energy-769352f695.headline: Amazon Announces USD 7 Billion Renewable Energy Investment Plan in India by 2030
climate-energy-769352f695.fulltext:
Amazon Announces USD 7 Billion Renewable Energy Investment Plan in India by 2030
Amazon plans to invest USD 7 billion in India's renewable energy sector by 2030, expanding its clean power portfolio through solar and wind projects.
✨ Key Takeaways
Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) has announced plans to invest an additional USD 7 billion, or approximately Rs 65,393 crore, in renewable energy initiatives across India by 2030. This multiyear investment is over and above the USD 4 billion worth of renewable energy projects already contracted by the company. The initiative aims to support Amazon's growing electricity requirements in India while expanding its clean energy portfolio.
As part of the announcement, Amazon unveiled four utility-scale renewable energy projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts (MW). These projects are spread across Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. The latest developments build on the company's existing renewable energy commitments in India, which include large-scale power generation projects and smaller Solar installations at its facilities. The additional USD 7 billion represents a planned investment over the coming years and is not an immediate capital outlay.
Amazon's renewable energy portfolio in India currently comprises 57 projects, including 14 utility-scale wind and solar projects and 43 on-site solar installations. The company has already contracted USD 4 billion in renewable energy projects, taking its total announced and contracted commitment, including the additional planned investment, to USD 11 billion. The newly announced projects are part of the previously contracted portfolio. The utility-scale projects under consideration are expected to have a combined capacity of more than 2 gigawatts once operational, marking a significant expansion of the company's clean electricity agreements in India.
The investment comes amid rising electricity consumption by large technology companies. Data centres, cloud infrastructure, warehouses and other operations require substantial amounts of electricity. Growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud computing is further increasing power requirements globally. Data centres need a continuous and reliable electricity supply to operate servers, cooling systems and networking infrastructure. Procuring renewable electricity can help companies reduce the carbon intensity of their energy consumption while supporting their sustainability objectives.
Amazon has set a global target of reducing the carbon intensity of electricity used in its operations by 65 per cent by 2030. India's expanding solar and wind energy capacity provides opportunities for the company to secure long-term renewable power supplies. Power purchase agreements can also provide greater visibility on a portion of future electricity costs.
Amazon's investment announcement could create opportunities for Indian renewable energy developers, equipment manufacturers and infrastructure companies. Large-scale renewable energy projects typically generate demand for solar modules, wind turbines, Transformers, electrical equipment, transmission systems and Construction services. Listed companies operating in these segments include Tata Power (NSE: TATAPOWER), NTPC (NSE: NTPC), Suzlon Energy (NSE: SUZLON) and Waaree Energies (NSE: WAAREEENER).
However, the announcement does not confirm that any of these companies has received project orders or supply contracts from Amazon. Any direct financial benefit would depend on confirmed orders, equipment supply agreements or other commercial arrangements. It would also be inappropriate to attribute movements in any individual stock solely to this announcement without supporting evidence from market activity and company disclosures.
Going forward, the economic impact of Amazon's investment will depend on project execution, the deployment of capital and the commissioning of renewable energy capacity. Long-term electricity procurement agreements from large corporations could support demand across India's clean energy industry. As Amazon continues expanding its digital services and infrastructure in the country, investments in electricity infrastructure could also become an important area of focus.

indian-startups-c9fb70562a.headline: IIT Delhi Alumnus’ Startup Sues Apple For ₹1,500 Cr Over NameDrop Patent Infringement
indian-startups-c9fb70562a.fulltext: What happens when two iPhones are brought close together? Users get to exchange contact details without typing or scanning a QR code with NameDrop. For GG Technologies, a startup founded by IIT Delhi alumnus Gaurav Goel in 2018, this feature is at the heart of a patent dispute which sees it lock horns with the tech giant Apple. GG, the parent company of contact-sharing app StayTouch, claims it developed and patented the underlying technology years before Apple introduced NameDrop in 2023. It has now approached the Bombay High Court (HC), alleging that the feature infringes its Indian patent. The startup has moved the court seeking directions that mandate Apple to disable NameDrop in India while the case is heard. Separately, GG Technologies is seeking ₹1,500 Cr in damages. As per its 781-page plaint and accompanying documents, accessed by Inc42, the startup has asked the court to direct Apple to switch off NameDrop in India, including through a software update, "to the extent technically feasible". Apple could continue selling its devices without the disputed feature. A Patent Versus An Ecosystem GG argues that Apple has a structural advantage because NameDrop is built into compatible devices, while StayTouch requires a separate app download. The startup claims this has hurt its ability to secure commercial partnerships, with prospective partners already being offered similar functionality by Apple. GG cited Apple's annual India sales crossing $10 Bn to illustrate its distribution scale, clarifying that this is not an estimate of NameDrop revenue. A chartered accountant's certificate puts GG's technical development and marketing expenditure between 2019 and 2025 at $2.75 Mn. The startup has sought ₹1,500 Cr in damages, calling it a conservative estimate. It says the final calculation would depend on device and revenue information held by Apple. However, the plaint does not provide an independent calculation supporting the claim. Inc42 has reached out to Apple for a response. How Similar Are The Two Technologies? The dispute centres on Indian Patent No. 546169, titled 'Method and System for Proximity-Based Contact Transfer', granted to GG on July 27, 2024. Its patent filings began in May 2019, while Apple announced NameDrop in June 2023. The patent describes a system that detects nearby devices, exchanges identifying information and allows users to accept or decline contact transfers. It also provides for a central server to maintain contact profiles and synchronise changes. GG alleges that NameDrop follows a similar process, citing proximity-based discovery, device identification, user consent and selective sharing. It also argues that Apple's iCloud infrastructure performs the central-server function described in the patent. Two expert reports commissioned by GG identify substantial technical similarities. However, neither expert had access to Apple's source code. The assessments rely on publicly available information and are not court-appointed findings. Therefore, Apple could contest whether NameDrop uses the same identifiers, server architecture or sequence of operations. GG launched StayTouch's global beta in July 2019 and showcased the product at Web Summit that year and CES in January 2020. It says it began exploring commercial partnerships in 2024 and commissioned technical assessments of NameDrop in February 2026. What Happens Next? GG's legal action against Apple extends beyond India. It filed a patent infringement suit in the US in April 2026, which has been stayed since September pending a separate US International Trade Commission (USITC) investigation. The commission instituted the investigation in August. A favourable ruling could restrict imports of infringing devices into the US. GG filed another US patent infringement suit against Apple on November 3, citing a separate patent. “When I conceived StayTouch in 2018, the idea was simple: make sharing contact information easier, faster and more intuitive,” Goel said. The Bombay High Court proceedings are ongoing. GG told Inc42 that the first hearing is yet to be scheduled.

work-careers-7865e5c456.headline: Recruiters say no to online hiring, return to offline placements amid AI cheating fears
work-careers-7865e5c456.fulltext:
Recruiters say no to online hiring, return to IIT campuses amid AI cheating fears
Campus placements, a practice largely abandoned in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic, are once again gaining momentum amid concerns over AI-fuelled cheating and malpractice. The share of recruiters opting for in-person hiring has risen to 60-70 per cent, up from 40-50 per cent last year. India Today spoke exclusively to several institutes to assess the current state of campus recruitment, and the details that emerged are telling.
Every year, companies visit college campuses in search of talent that can serve their organisations in the long run. For students, these recruitment drives offer an opportunity to secure jobs, often with attractive pay packages.
However, the hiring process, which moved largely online after the Covid-19 pandemic, is once again witnessing a shift towards in-person assessments and interviews. Concerns over impersonation, cheating and the use of unauthorised assistance during online recruitment have prompted companies to reconsider the process.
Several Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), including newer gen IITs, have reported a growing preference among recruiters for offline placement drives.
Responses received by India Today from several institutes indicate that companies are increasingly seeking to conduct recruitment activities in person, particularly for the 2026-27 placement cycle.
The change comes at a time when online hiring has become an established part of campus recruitment. The format allowed companies to conduct assessments across institutions without the need for physical visits and helped expand the reach of recruitment drives.
A recent report by Mint also pointed to this change, noting that several IITs had confirmed a preference among recruiters for in-person tests and interviews for the batch of 2027.
According to the report, the proportion of companies opting for such a format has risen to 60–70 per cent, compared with 40–50 per cent in the previous year.
"Industry reporting has highlighted instances involving impersonation, external assistance and unauthorised use of AI tools during assessments," told Professor Daviender Narang, Director, Jaipuria Institute of Management Ghaziabad to India Today.
The concerns are not limited to the examination stage.
Online interviews have also raised questions about candidates receiving assistance from others, sharing questions or using tools that may not be permitted during the selection process.
In the wake of industry, as tech giants have religiously said, programmers are already using AI to write code.
ONLINE HIRING FACES QUESTIONS OVER VERIFICATION
Speaking to India Today, Dr Dharmendra Kumar Chand, Professor-in-Charge, Career Development Cell, BIT Mesra, said the institute does not consider online assessments inherently unreliable, nor does it view offline testing as the only solution.
He, however, acknowledged that online recruitment can present challenges, including impersonation, unauthorised assistance, sharing of questions and other forms of malpractice.
The recruitment process has also become more complex with the growing use of AI tools.
While such tools have found a place in coding and programming, the use of them during assessments has raised concerns.
Companies generally conduct multiple rounds of selection during campus placements.
These may include initial aptitude and technical assessments, followed by interviews, group discussions or problem-solving exercises, depending on the requirements of the recruiter.
While the initial rounds are often conducted online, the later stages may require direct interaction with candidates.
The use of online platforms, as shared with India Today by several institutes, has also led recruiters to introduce additional safeguards. These include identity checks, webcam and microphone monitoring, browser restrictions and screen activity tracking.
INSTITUTES STRENGTHEN CHECKS DURING PLACEMENT PROCESS
Institutes, meanwhile, have their own procedures to ensure that students taking part in campus recruitment meet the prescribed eligibility criteria and follow the rules of the selection process.
At BIT and IITs, the placement process includes verification of students' credentials through supporting documents and faculty coordinators.
Academic details, including CGPA and backlogs, are obtained directly from the institute's enterprise resource planning (ERP) system rather than being entered independently by students.
The institute also uses its official placement portal to verify students' eligibility against the criteria set by recruiters.
For assessments conducted on campus, the Institutes provides computer and internet facilities.
The placement guidelines restrict students from carrying mobile phones and other personal belongings into examination halls and computer laboratories during written and online tests.
The institute also noted that recruiters may use technology-based safeguards, depending on the assessment platform and their requirements.
These include AI-enabled remote proctoring, webcam and microphone monitoring, browser lockdown, screen activity tracking, identity verification and alerts for suspicious activity.
The return of companies to IIT and other campuses does not, therefore, mark a rejection of online recruitment altogether.
Rather, it points to the efforts being made by recruiters and institutions to address the limitations of a process in the AI age that became common during the pandemic.

work-careers-d79be81614.headline: Bosch Maintains Silence On Reported TCS Deal Involving India Technology Operations
work-careers-d79be81614.fulltext:
A Mint report said TCS was in early discussions to acquire part of Bosch’s India technology and product development operations
                        
Bosch has declined to comment on reports of a potential transfer of part of its India technology and product development operations to Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), a transaction that could involve up to 3,000 employees.In an official statement shared with People Matters in response to the reports, Bosch Group in India said it was refraining from commenting on what it described as market speculation and unverified statements.
“In reference to the recent news articles published around the potential sale of part of Bosch India operations, we would like to clearly state that Bosch Group in India refrains from commenting on market speculations and unverified statements,” the company said.The statement does not confirm whether discussions are underway or whether a transaction is being considered. Bosch has also not disclosed any details regarding a potential transfer of employees.
What The Reported Deal Involves
According to a Mint report published on 19 November, TCS was in early discussions to acquire part of Bosch’s India technology and product development operations. The proposed transaction could involve the transfer of up to 3,000 employees.
The report indicated that discussions could move to the board level next month, although the scope and terms of the potential transaction remain unclear.The reported move comes as Bosch considers transferring some technology and product development activities as part of its cost-containment efforts. For TCS, the acquisition could expand its engineering talent pool and capabilities in areas linked to emerging technologies, including physical artificial intelligence (AI), which refers to the application of AI in machines and physical systems such as robots and autonomous vehicles.
Bosch’s Technology Workforce In India
Bosch established its Indian technology operations in Bengaluru in 1997 through Bosch Global Software Technologies (BGSW), later expanding to Hyderabad, Pune and Coimbatore.According to Mint’s report, Bosch’s global global capability centre (GCC) workforce stands at 28,900, with India accounting for approximately four-fifths of the total. Bengaluru is reported to account for around half of the employees, with the remaining workforce spread across Hyderabad, Pune and Coimbatore.
The reported transaction concerns Bosch’s technology and product development operations and is distinct from the business of listed Bosch , India’s automotive components manufacturer.
TCS’s Recent Acquisition Activity
The potential transaction would come amid TCS’s efforts to expand through acquisitions of captive technology centres and consulting operations.Recent deals cited in the report include the acquisition of Best Buy’s India technology centre in October and the acquisition of Porsche-owned consulting firm MHP for US$373 million in August. TCS has also secured a five-year, US$1.45 billion contract for Porsche’s IT modernisation.
The transfer of captive technology operations can provide IT services companies with access to established engineering teams and longer-term client engagements. However, integrating employees from such centres can also create margin pressures, particularly where existing salary structures are higher.The Bosch-TCS discussions remain unconfirmed. Bosch’s statement does not establish whether negotiations are underway, while the reported employee transfer, scope of operations and potential deal terms remain uncertain.

agritech-8a409bffe9.headline: John Deere Orchard Robotics deal signals growing value of actionable farm data, says ag robotics OG
agritech-8a409bffe9.fulltext:
John Deere has acquired AI-powered crop intelligence firm Orchard Robotics to complement its precision agriculture, equipment, and farm technology operations.
The deal—terms of which were not disclosed—is the latest in a string of acquisitions in the ag robotics space from Deere, which acquired Blue River Technology (See & Spray tech) in 2017, Bear Flag Robotics (autonomous tractors) in 2021, Sentera (drone imagery and AI-powered crop intelligence) and GUSS Automation (autonomous sprayers for orchards and vineyards) in 2025.
“This connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” said Deere director, farm systems innovation, Tim Marquis.
“By bringing these capabilities together, we have an opportunity to help growers make more informed decisions across their operations and get more value from the technology they already rely on.”
Orchard founder Charles Wu said Orchard will continue operating as a Deere subsidiary with its existing team and products. “Orchard will be the same team you’ve always known, you’ll still come straight to us… As we grow and expand our capabilities, you’ll be able to do more with our tech than ever before. Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI farming capabilities to every farmer out there.”
Ag robotics OG Jorge Heraud, who sold Blue River to Deere for $305 million in 2017 and went on to become Deere’s VP automation and autonomy, told AgFunderNews that the deal was “further validation that large companies in agriculture are finding that actionable data is very valuable to farmers.
“This is a trend that will continue, driven by cheaper cameras and new sensors paired with AI to process the data and produce novel insights. Smart, innovative teams are able to find and bring valuable solutions to market faster than ever.”
Reservoir Farms CEO: Deal shows exits are real in rugged AI space
In a LinkedIn post on the deal, agronomist-turned-ag researcher and advisor Shane Thomas of Upstream Ag Insights added: “Orchard was founded in 2022 and raised its $22 million Series A only about a year ago, so this doesn’t look like a distressed sale and likely suggests a nine-figure exit for the team and investors.
“Orchard gives Deere the plant-by-plant crop vision in orchards and vineyards that Blue River and See & Spray gave it in row crops, and paired with GUSS autonomy and Smart Apply sprayers, Deere can now see, decide and execute in permanent crops.”
Danny Bernstein, CEO at ag robotics innovation hub Reservoir Farms, said the transaction amounted to “a strong signal that super intelligence is strategic for the future of agriculture.”
It’s also great news for startups, he added: “There’s a real exit path in rugged, outdoor physical AI. What comes next is more partnerships between incumbents, focused teams that prove value in the field, and the next wave of startups that build the components and data layers plugging into those platforms. At Reservoir Farms we see that playing out daily with 40+ startups prototyping on our working farms.”
‘Your average grower does not want to be, nor should they be, a data analyst’
Founded in 2022, Orchard has an AI-powered camera system that mounts onto tractors and other farm vehicles and captures millions of images as they travel through orchards and vineyards, measuring everything from fruit counts, size and color to growth rates, canopy health, water stress, disease and yield.
Images are processed on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson computer because many farms lack the connectivity required to upload terabytes of raw imagery. The resulting information feeds into Orchard’s FruitScope platform, where growers can inspect conditions down to the level of individual trees, Wu told AgFunderNews at the recent Ruggedize ag robotics conference at Reservoir Farms in Salinas.
“Data is only useful if there is an actual use for that data, and it’s not just a fancy map on screen,” said Wu, who said the firm has worked in apples, wine grapes, table grapes, cherries, blueberries, almonds, pistachios, and citrus, and has “hundreds of systems” in the field.
“Data is only useful if a grower has a mechanism of taking an action on that data easily. Your average grower does not want to be, nor should they be, a data analyst.”
He added: “We’re not actually selling hardware. We’re not even selling software. We’re not even selling data. We’re selling the outcome that a grower sees by using all of it effectively.”
‘The biggest ROI is through reduction on labor and inputs’
While some farms have precision sprayers and spreaders that can automatically vary applications based on insights from Orchard’s platform, others opt to receive instructions directly to workers in the field via a mobile app showing them where to go and what action to take.
“The biggest ROI is through reduction on labor and inputs,” said Wu. But supply-chain planning is another significant source of value, he said. As the platform can predict yields with 95%+ accuracy, this can inform decisions around how much labor to hire, how many bins to procure, storage requirements and what sales and marketing teams can promise customers.
Orchard started in apples but has since expanded into grapes, cherries, blueberries, almonds, pistachios and citrus, and is now exploring moves into olives and stone fruit.
It currently has “hundreds of systems in the field” and is scanning tens of thousands of acres.
Most customers are currently in the US, but Wu says Orchard is also seeing “some pretty tremendous pull internationally,” with plans to push further into Latin America and Australia with Deere’s resources behind it.
From crop intelligence to action: Variable-rate spraying in apple orchards
Speaking to AgFunderNews this afternoon, Deere director, farm systems innovation, Tim Marquis, outlined how the two companies could combine their technologies.
One example is variable-rate spraying for bloom thinning in apple orchards, where growers apply chemicals to remove excess blossoms and manage the number of apples developing on individual trees. Too many blossoms can result in an excessive number of small apples that fail to meet market requirements, while overly aggressive thinning can reduce yields and revenues.
By using Orchard’s cameras to monitor blossoms as they develop, growers could generate maps showing where more or less thinning is required, then feed that information directly to Deere’s equipment to adjust application rates on a tree-by-tree basis, said Marquis.
“We’re able to see these blossoms as they’re budding, categorize them, and then build a variable rate map that we can pass directly to the machine.”
The companies envisage connecting Orchard’s FruitScope platform with Deere’s Operations Center and variable-rate application controllers, enabling growers to move from collecting crop intelligence to automatically acting on it in the field.
More precise chemical thinning could also reduce the need for subsequent manual thinning, in which workers physically remove excess fruitlets to optimize crop loads.

world-158994b8ae.headline: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
world-158994b8ae.fulltext:
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

BloombergPublished21 Nov 2026, 03:34 PM IST
(Bloomberg) -- Taiwan widened curbs on short sales of local stocks and said it has been buying shares, stepping up efforts to revive confidence after the island’s benchmark index had its worst weekly fall in 35 years.
The Financial Supervisory Commission imposed a blanket ban on short selling below the previous trading day’s closing price, covering both margin short sales and borrowed shares, it said in a statement Saturday. Separately, the island’s NT$500 billion ($15 billion) National Financial Stabilization Fund said it has entered the market to support Taiwanese stocks and urged investors to remain confident.
The regulator’s move, which takes effect on Nov. 23, marks the third time this month that authorities have unveiled short-selling curbs to tame market volatility. Taiwan’s tech-heavy stock market has witnessed heavy selloffs as the global artificial intelligence trade came under strain, sending the island’s benchmark to its worst week since 1991.
The FSC also raised the minimum margin requirement for short sales to 150% from 130%, and temporarily suspended the acceptance of applications from securities firms to list new put warrants, it said in a statement. Short sales by securities and futures companies for business-related hedging purposes are exempt from the new ban.
Two earlier rounds of short-selling restrictions this month have so far failed to stabilize the market. On Friday, Taiwanese stocks slumped 6.2%, taking its losses for the week to almost 18%, as doubts over whether returns can justify the vast sums poured into AI sent tech shares tumbling across Asia.
The FSC said it will continue monitoring international developments and Taiwan’s domestic capital markets and will adjust the stabilization measures as appropriate. It also urged investors to remain prudent and respond rationally in accordance with their own investment strategies.
The Ministry of Finance, which oversees the stabilization fund, meanwhile stated that Taiwan’s macro fundamentals remain strong, citing record performances on economic and export growth. The economy expanded 14.4% in the third quarter, while data Friday showed October’s export orders rose 78% from a year earlier.
“Recent concerns over potentially tighter US regulation of artificial intelligence, the returns on massive capital expenditures, company-specific factors and margin-financing risks have raised doubts about the outlook for the AI industry, triggering several days of sharp declines in US stocks and spilling over into Taiwan and other Asian markets,” the fund said in a statement.
The stock stabilization fund said it has been buying shares to support the market since Nov. 6.
“While foreign investors have been net sellers of Taiwan stocks for several consecutive sessions, the scale of selling has gradually eased,” it said.

science-mind-0abed5009a.headline: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
science-mind-0abed5009a.fulltext:
A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.
The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.
Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI.
Advertisement
“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof.
Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.
Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.
However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.”
Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems!” says James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London. “I suppose most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. What is both unsettling and tremendously exciting, is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results. It is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.”
Alpöge has been involved in a number of recent discoveries involving AI. In July, he announced that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof.
He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution.
Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after. “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier,” he writes, saying that he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that “there was a constraint to respect” before the announcement could be made.

global-economics-da120e1db3.headline: CrowdStrike’s Talks with Zscaler Show AI-Led Cyber Consolidation
global-economics-da120e1db3.fulltext:
BloombergPublished22 Nov 2026, 01:03 AM IST
(Bloomberg) -- A wave of multibillion-dollar takeovers is reshaping the cybersecurity industry as the biggest companies race to expand their defenses against increasingly sophisticated attacks powered by artificial intelligence.
CrowdStrike Holdings Inc.’s talks to acquire Zscaler Inc. in what could be one of the industry’s largest deals would bring together two major players in different corners of the $244 billion security market, accelerating a shift toward a smaller number of companies protecting more of the world’s computers and networks.
The two companies are discussing a potential combination that could come together soon, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified because the information is confidential. Deliberations are ongoing, and there’s no certainty they’ll result in a transaction, the people said. Representatives for CrowdStrike and Zscaler didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Austin, Texas-based CrowdStrike, a leading maker of software that protects personal computers and servers, has benefited from rising demand for cybersecurity products. Its shares have surged alongside those of other major providers, including Palo Alto Networks Inc. and Cloudflare Inc., as businesses grapple with the risks posed by AI-enabled attacks.
Zscaler, based in Santa Clara, California, has seen its fortunes move in the opposite direction. Its stock has dropped more than 13% this year despite rapidly growing revenue that reached a record $3.35 billion in fiscal 2026. The company has yet to turn an annual profit since going public in 2018.
Yet Zscaler’s technology fills what cybersecurity experts say is a critical gap in protecting corporate networks. Its cloud-based products replace traditional virtual private networks, or VPNs, that employees use to remotely access their employers’ systems.
Legacy VPN products from companies including Citrix and Ivanti Inc. have been repeatedly targeted by suspected Chinese and other state-sponsored hackers, Bloomberg has reported.
Zscaler’s software gives companies greater control over who can access their networks and applications, reducing the risk that an intruder who gains access to one system can move freely through others. Traditional VPN products, which often rely on dedicated hardware inside corporate networks, can also be difficult to update quickly when serious security flaws emerge.
That approach has helped drive Zscaler’s growth. But the company has also been caught up in a different set of AI-related fears: a potential “SaaSpocalypse,” in which AI tools could allow competitors to recreate software services more easily and cheaply, threatening the business models of established providers.
Zscaler’s reach, however, would be difficult to replicate. The company says it serves roughly 11,000 customers globally, including more than half of the Fortune 500 and operates in more than 185 countries, blocking billions of policy violations and malicious threats each day.
Zscaler, which had a market value of $32 billion at the end of regular trading Friday, rose about 16% after the close. CrowdStrike, one of the industry’s most valuable companies, has a market capitalization of around $235 billion.
A combination would give CrowdStrike a much broader role in defending corporate networks. Its flagship Falcon product already has an extensive presence on personal computers, laptops and servers, a reach exposed by a botched software update in 2024 that triggered a global IT meltdown.
Adding Zscaler would extend that presence to the systems that control access to corporate networks and applications, allowing CrowdStrike to monitor potential threats across more parts of a company’s technology infrastructure.
In cybersecurity, the more visibility a provider has into activity across devices, applications and networks, the better positioned it is to detect suspicious behavior and block attacks. That capability is becoming increasingly valuable as AI changes the nature and volume of internet traffic.
The rise of autonomous AI agents, which can perform tasks online without direct human intervention, has added to the challenge. Their growing presence makes it harder for security systems to distinguish legitimate automated activity from malicious traffic.
In June, Cloudflare co-founder Matthew Prince said in a post on X that traffic generated by AI agents had surpassed human traffic on the internet for the first time.
Alphabet Inc.’s Google struck a $32 billion deal to acquire cybersecurity startup Wiz last year, while ServiceNow Inc. agreed in December to buy Armis for $7.75 billion. Palo Alto Networks completed its $25 billion takeover of CyberArk in February and this month agreed to acquire AI software company Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion.
The potential CrowdStrike-Zscaler deal also follows a series of technology outages in the US this month affecting Microsoft Corp., JPMorgan Chase & Co., United Airlines and the National Security Agency, as well as disruptions to air travel. Although those incidents have been blamed on equipment and system failures rather than cyberattacks, they have highlighted the potential consequences of widespread technology disruptions.
Fears about AI-assisted hacking have been a boon for the cybersecurity industry. Market researcher Gartner Inc. projects that global spending on information security will grow nearly 12% this year to $244 billion.

Google said the funding will support expanded AI training and curriculum development for students, faculty members and teachers.

Capacity building means strengthening the resources, skills and technological systems needed to conduct research effectively.
In practical terms, it could involve improving the institute’s AI research frameworks, software tools and supporting infrastructure.
These resources are important because advanced AI research requires specialised computing tools, reliable technical support and researchers trained to use them.

Those details will depend on how the institute and Google implement the programme.

India is seeking to expand its domestic AI capabilities while building a workforce equipped to develop and use emerging technologies.

Google committed $5 million to IIT Kharagpur to expand advanced AI research in Indic languages, materials science, and campus computing infrastructure.
Google committed $5 million (approximately ₹46 crore) to the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur on November 21, 2026, during its 75th Foundation Day celebrations to accelerate advanced artificial intelligence research across Indic languages, materials science, agriculture, and educational technology, per the Google announcement. The multi-year grant funds faculty initiatives, student training, and campus compute capacity, establishing an operational model for corporate-academic research partnerships across Indian technical universities.
Google $5 Million AI Commitment Unveiled at IIT Kharagpur Platinum Jubilee
The grant was formally announced during the Platinum Jubilee celebrations marking the 75th Foundation Day of IIT Kharagpur in West Bengal. Envisioned through collaborative planning between the institute and Google leadership, the initiative establishes a direct philanthropic and technical research alliance between the global technology firm and India’s oldest Indian Institute of Technology. The funding provides untied institutional grant support intended to deepen basic and applied AI capabilities rather than commercial product development, with disbursements channeled into university research laboratories, computational upgrades, and specialized academic programs.
According to Business Standard coverage, the financial package of ₹46 crore will support university investigators across four primary scientific problem areas while underwriting open computational infrastructure for students and faculty. The announcement coincided with high-profile national milestone events at the Kharagpur campus, attended by senior government dignitaries, academic leaders, and alumni delegations who gathered to review the institute’s research trajectory.
Three Pillars of the Grant: Research Focus, Education, and AI Infrastructure
The $5 million commitment is structured across three core operational pillars designed to build durable research capacity across multiple academic departments:
Advanced AI Research: Deploying applied artificial intelligence methods to address domain-specific challenges in Indic natural language processing, materials discovery, precision agriculture, and scalable educational technology.
Educational Opportunities and Curriculum Modernization: Designing new AI curricula, sponsoring specialized pedagogical workshops, and funding hands-on training tracks for undergraduate students, postgraduate scholars, faculty members, and secondary school educators.
AI Capacity Building and Compute Tooling: Upgrading campus-wide server architectures, high-performance computing clusters, machine learning frameworks, and engineering tooling to support intensive model training and evaluation.
The following table summarizes the grant allocations, technical focus areas, and institutional deliverables outlined across the three core pillars:
Under the advanced research pillar, the Indic language track will address data scarcity across low-resource Indian languages, developing multimodal benchmarks, tokenizers, and translation models. In materials science, researchers will apply machine learning to molecular property prediction and novel composite synthesis. Agricultural applications will focus on edge-deployable computer vision models for crop disease detection and soil moisture modeling, while educational technology work will target personalized tutoring architectures adapted for multilingual classrooms.
Institutional Context and Google Academic Collaborations in India
IIT Kharagpur holds a foundational position in Indian higher education. Established in 1951 at the site of the historic Hijli Detention Camp, it served as the template for India’s network of national institutes of technology. Google and Alphabet Chief Executive Officer Sundar Pichai is one of the institute’s most prominent alumni, having completed his Bachelor of Technology degree in Metallurgical Engineering at Kharagpur in 1993 before continuing postgraduate studies in the United States.
The $5 million grant expands upon earlier research ties between the company and the institute. Google previously collaborated with IIT Kharagpur under its Project Amplify initiative, which concentrated on creating open acoustic and text corpora to improve speech recognition and natural language understanding for regional Indian dialects. The new funding mechanism expands this relationship from a discrete project engagement into a broad, multi-disciplinary institutional program. Leadership Perspectives from Pichai and Chakraborty
Institute leadership and corporate executives highlighted the strategic significance of long-term academic funding during the Platinum Jubilee ceremonies. Google CEO Sundar Pichai emphasized the enduring personal and institutional influence of the university, stating that IIT Kharagpur is driving ground-breaking work in Indic languages, agriculture, and education, and expressing enthusiasm for accelerating that impact to shape the path for the next generation of students just as the institute shaped his own career.
IIT Kharagpur Director Prof. Suman Chakraborty noted that the applied research framework had been conceptualized in close consultation with Pichai to align philanthropic corporate capital with urgent domestic technological priorities. Reporting by Fortune India emphasized that the funding is structured to empower faculty investigators to tackle large-scale challenges that cannot be resolved through short-term departmental budgets alone. In national broadcast coverage, DD News report highlighted that the grant reinforces the national objective of expanding technical artificial intelligence competencies beyond metropolitan tech centers into premier public research institutions across India.
Implications for University Research Offices and Sponsored Research Administration
Corporate grants of this scale introduce distinct governance, financial administration, and compliance considerations for university research offices. Sponsored projects involving unrestricted or programmatic corporate gifts require careful boundary management to protect academic independence, data stewardship, and publication freedom. Research administration teams managing comparable gifts should examine established institutional practices for industry-university research partnership structures and the precise drafting required in a formal sponsored research agreement.
Specific compliance and operational priorities for research offices include:
Intellectual Property and Licensing Terms: Ensuring that research outputs generated under philanthropic or unrestricted corporate gifts remain within university ownership or enter open-source distribution, preventing exclusive rights assignment to the commercial sponsor. Sponsored research teams should guard against overreaching IP covenants and verify standard terms using publication delay and review clauses in sponsored research to guarantee that graduate students can publish theses without corporate veto.
Compute Resource Governance: Structuring access protocols for corporate compute frameworks and on-premise hardware accelerators. Sponsored research offices must ensure compute time is equitably distributed across interdisciplinary project teams rather than monopolized by individual labs, while preventing mandatory lock-in to proprietary cloud APIs.
Data Sovereignty and Compliance: Managing agricultural sensor data, local soil mappings, and Indic linguistic field recordings under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP Act). Research offices must establish Institutional Review Board (IRB) and data governance protocols for collecting regional audio recordings and community-generated dialect samples to ensure valid informed consent and secure data residency.
Curricular and Faculty Cross-Appointment: Administering interdepartmental curriculum development boards that bridge Computer Science and engineering disciplines like metallurgy, agricultural engineering, and humanities, ensuring teaching credits and faculty incentives are properly allocated.
Next Steps and Implementation Milestones
Following the Platinum Jubilee announcement, IIT Kharagpur and Google will establish a joint steering committee to oversee fund disbursements, project milestones, and infrastructural procurement schedules throughout the 2026–2027 academic cycle. Initial tranches will be directed toward campus high-performance computing hardware upgrades and establishing dedicated machine learning lab facilities within the computer science and multidisciplinary engineering complexes.
Faculty application windows for competitive internal seed grants across the four target domains—Indic languages, materials science, agriculture, and educational technology—are scheduled to open in the coming term. Pilot deployments of agricultural diagnostic tools and localized language translation modules are slated for preliminary field trials by mid-2027, with corresponding curriculum updates for undergraduate artificial intelligence courses rolling out across incoming student cohorts.

The collaboration also covers datasets for specific use cases, including healthcare and safety, across multiple Indic languages. It aims to address gaps in existing AI models, which often lack sufficient regional language data and cultural context. French Robotics Startup Genesis Raises $500 Million in Series A, Valuation Soars to $3.5 Billion with Nvidia Participating
French artificial intelligence robotics startup Genesis AI announced on Tuesday (the 17th) that it has completed a $500 million Series A funding round at a post-money valuation of $3.5 billion, marking one of the largest funding rounds in Europe's robotics sector. The round was co-led by Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest and Eclipse, with Nvidia, France's state investment bank Bpifrance, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and French telecom tycoon Xavier Niel all listed among the investors.
The company, headquartered in France with an additional office in San Carlos, California, had just completed a $105 million seed round in July last year. Its valuation has jumped significantly in just over a year, reflecting continued enthusiasm in capital markets for AI-enabled industrial automation.
Funds Earmarked for Eno Mass Production and Dexterous Hands
Genesis CEO Zhou Xian said the new funding will primarily be invested in expanding production capacity for the flagship general-purpose robot "Eno," scaling up data collection and AI model training, and strengthening the robot's ability to precisely manipulate objects with its hands. He stated plainly that the company is concentrating its R&D efforts on what the industry considers the most technically challenging component: the "dexterous hand."
Eno's body design takes a non-humanoid approach, featuring a three-segment folding structure that resembles an enlarged playing card, with a rotatable wheeled base at the bottom. It can compress into a compact space when stored and rise to near-human height when operating. Asked why the company did not adopt a more human-like appearance, Zhou gave a blunt reason: "I don't understand why a robot needs a head, because the brain isn't there."
Genesis was co-founded by former Mistral AI researcher Théophile Gervet and develops AI algorithms, hardware and training systems in an integrated manner to shorten testing cycles. Actuators, motors, reducers and dexterous hands are all designed in-house, while the computing core uses Nvidia chips.
U.S. First, Expanded Deployment in 2027
On market strategy, Zhou noted that the company will prioritize the United States initially, planning to build a domestic supply chain, engage contract manufacturers and secure American customers before expanding to other European markets. Genesis is currently collaborating with South Korea's LG CNS to conduct small-scale testing of Eno in manufacturing and logistics scenarios, and expects to fully expand customer deployments in 2027.
Currently, Genesis has produced only 30 to 40 Eno units, which are being trialed by a small number of customers. The company plans to launch large-scale production in the United States next year. Hardware durability remains an unresolved challenge, as existing dexterous hands need replacement after several weeks of daily use. The company intends to first target manufacturing, logistics and laboratory settings before gradually expanding to home applications.
Genesis's technical approach differs from most humanoid robot developers. It has developed a special sensor glove that workers wear during normal work to record finger movements, contact forces and first-person camera views. Because the robot's hand structure and dimensions closely resemble human hands, it can directly learn from this data. More than 100 workers worldwide are currently participating in data collection, which is used to train the robot model GENE and then conduct large-scale rehearsals through the Genesis World simulation system.
The company has previously demonstrated robots slicing tomatoes, cracking eggs and playing the piano. More recently, it had a robotic arm complete an entire workflow of scanning codes, packing boxes, sealing boxes and applying labels, though the second demonstration saw a box dropped and labels torn unevenly. The on-site demonstration that day did not feature the flagship Eno model, and the company did not show Eno's actual operation to the public.
Europe's Robot Unicorn Ranks Expand
Genesis's fundraising achievement places it among European robotics companies valued at over $1 billion. This group has been growing in recent years, including the UK's Humanoid and Germany's Neura Robotics, Agile Robots and RobCo, all targeting industrial operation scenarios.
Analysts note that this wave of funding reflects the intersection of two forces: first, AI models are enabling robots to move from fixed programmed motions to learnable general-purpose operations; second, labor shortages in European and American manufacturing and pressure to localize supply chains are driving up capital expenditure on factory automation. Nvidia's participation as a strategic investor also signals that chip suppliers are using equity investments to consolidate their influence in the robotics ecosystem.
However, robotics startups still face hurdles in moving from demonstrations to mass production. Taking Genesis as an example, the rapid wear of dexterous hands, the flagship model's lack of public live operation demonstrations and customers remaining at small-scale testing are all variables that must be overcome in the commercialization process. Whether the company can achieve volume deployment on schedule in 2027 will be the key moment for testing the reasonableness of this $3.5 billion valuation.

Crew evacuated amid battle to put out fire on Russian ship hit by drones
Finnish authorities say two drones attack cargo ship that has links to Russia’s armed forces.
The crew of a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland, hit by drones likely launched by Ukraine, has now been evacuated to a nearby cargo ship and will reportedly be taken directly back to Russia.
Finnish authorities say the Sparta II has links to Russia’s armed forces and is currently anchored off the southern Finnish town of Loviisa, where firefighting efforts are still ongoing at sea.
Operations at the scene, involving extinguishing the fire on board the Sparta II and cooling the vessel, are being carried out by rescue units and patrol ships from the Finnish Border Guard, a patrol aircraft and helicopters. Two Finnish civilian rescue tugs are also involved, as well as an Estonian navy patrol ship.
“At the request of the Border Guard, the Russian rescue ship Murman is also participating in the rescue operations,” Finnish authorities said in a statement.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen told the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper that the Sparta II would be towed out of Finland’s territorial waters on Saturday night.
How the attack unfolded
On Saturday morning, Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with initial reports saying the ship had sustained damage. Finnish Border Guard units were dispatched to the scene, and a photograph taken by a Finnish patrol plane showed flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the ship.
The attack happened west of Gogland Island, off the coast of the Finnish town of Loviisa, and Finland quickly implemented temporary air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.
A Russian helicopter has since violated Finnish airspace, venturing more than 4km (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.
“The suspected airspace violation is possibly related to rescue or tracking operations of a damaged cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. The Defence Forces and the Border Guard are handling the situation in cooperation with other authorities,” said Hakkanen.
By Saturday afternoon, the Finnish Defence Forces said the strike was likely carried out by Ukraine. Earlier, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X that “war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity. The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor”.
What do we know about Sparta II?
Finland’s Border Guard said the Sparta II is known to have links to Russia’s armed forces. The roll-on/roll-off ship was built in the year 2000 and sails under a Russian flag, according to the VesselFinder website.
“At the moment, there is no confirmed information about what cargo is on board, but it cannot be ruled out that there is military materiel on board,” said Commander Ilja Iljin from the Finnish Border Guard.
The governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said earlier on Saturday that damage to the ship had yet to be fully assessed.
“Three nautical miles [5.6km] from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max, shortly after the attack.
Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.
One of the major risks of attacking any vessel is environmental damage if it leaks or sinks, a scenario that Baltic Sea nations treat with high importance. That risk is “further amplified by the poor state of some of the so-called ‘Shadow Fleet’ tankers” that Russia operates, according to Robin Haggblom, senior adviser for Risk Intelligence and an expert in Finnish maritime issues.
“Actions to prevent environmental damage has also been emphasised in Finnish Border Guard communication regarding this event. Luckily in this case, we don’t yet have ice coverage in the Gulf of Finland, which would impact any oil spill recovery efforts that may be needed,” Haggblom told Al Jazeera.
Crowded shipping lanes
The narrow and shallow waters of the Baltic Sea are some of the most crowded shipping lanes in the world. The Helsinki to Tallinn ferry route had 7.5 million passenger crossings last year. Other passenger routes link Baltic ports and capital cities, and cargo vessels and military shipping contribute to the total number of vessels in the relatively small body of water.
So if Ukraine is using drones – maritime or aerial – to hit Russian ships, there could be risks to civilian vessels.
“There obviously always is a risk of collateral damage. However, so far Ukraine does seem to be taking a number of steps to minimise the risks involved, with the Sparta II, for example, apparently having been identified and hit a handful of kilometres from Russian waters,” added Haggblom.
Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki later said it had raised concerns with Kyiv about strikes in the area.
“It is the same with the strike on the Russian corvette earlier, where it is reported the Ukrainians were able to pick it out and target that specific vessel among perhaps a dozen other ships. There are also unconfirmed indications that Sparta II was targeted specifically, and not just as a general Russia-associated merchant vessel,” Haggblom added.
Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.
